Empirical formula.q: Which formula is already an empirical formula?
wrong: N₂O₄, because it is the formula chemists use most often for this nitrogen oxide
Empirical formula.exp: 2 and 5 share no factor, so N₂O₅ is already in lowest terms.

Empirical formula.q: What is the empirical formula of C₆H₁₂O₆?
wrong: C₆H₁₂O₆, because a formula is always already written in its simplest ratio

Molecular formula.q: Hydrogen peroxide molecules each contain 2 H and 2 O atoms. What is its molecular formula?
wrong: HO, because a molecular formula is always reduced to the smallest whole-number ratio
Molecular formula.exp: A molecular formula shows every atom actually present.

Molecular formula.q: N₂O₄ and NO₂ have the same empirical formula. What's different?
wrong: Their empirical formulas, because N₂O₄ has twice as many atoms in each molecule as NO₂
Molecular formula.exp: Same ratio, different real atom counts.

Ionic formulas are simplified.q: Calcium (Ca²⁺) and oxide (O²⁻) crisscross to Ca₂O₂. What do you write?
wrong: Ca₂O₂, because the crisscross method always gives the final formula without any changes
Ionic formulas are simplified.exp: Ionic formulas are written in lowest terms.

Ionic formulas are simplified.q: Which formula breaks the rule for ionic compounds?
wrong: MgCl₂, because it has a subscript of two on the chloride ion but not on magnesium
Ionic formulas are simplified.exp: Mg₂O₂ should be reduced to MgO.

Covalent formulas are not reduced.q: A student reduces dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄, to NO₂. What's wrong?
wrong: Nothing is wrong, because every chemical formula must be written in its lowest whole-number ratio
Covalent formulas are not reduced.exp: Prefixes give exact atom counts; NO₂ is nitrogen dioxide, a different molecule.

Covalent formulas are not reduced.q: Which formula should NOT be reduced, even though it could be?
wrong: Ca₂O₂, because calcium and oxygen are both elements that form ions of the same size
Covalent formulas are not reduced.exp: Covalent formulas keep the counts their prefixes give.

Ionic bond.q: Which pair of elements would form an ionic bond?
wrong: Carbon and oxygen, because both of them are found in the air that people breathe every day

Ionic bond.q: When magnesium and sulfur combine, what forms?
wrong: A covalent compound, because both elements are solids at room temperature and share electrons
Mg is a metal; it gives electrons.
Ionic bond.exp: Your practice test: Mg + S → ionic compound.

Covalent bond.q: Which compound is held together by covalent bonds?
wrong: NaCl, because table salt is one of the most common compounds that people use every day

Covalent bond.q: Why does CO₂ get prefixes in its name but CaCl₂ doesn't?
Covalent bond.right: CO₂ is two nonmetals sharing electrons
wrong: CaCl₂ is a covalent compound, so the prefixes are left off of its name when it is written
Covalent bond.exp: Covalent compounds use prefixes; ionic compounds don't.

Electrostatic force of attraction.q: Why are ionic bonds stronger than covalent bonds?
wrong: Because ionic compounds always contain more atoms than any covalent compound does
Electrostatic force of attraction.exp: Your notes: electrostatic attraction between cation and anion.

Electrostatic force of attraction.q: In NaCl, what holds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together?
wrong: Shared pairs of electrons between the sodium atom and the chlorine atom, like in water
NaOH, because it has a metal and a nonmetal and those always form a binary compound

Binary compound.q: Which kinds of compounds are always binary?
wrong: Compounds with a polyatomic ion, because they are made of a metal bonded to an ion
Binary compound.exp: Your notes: Types I, II and III (metal + nonmetal, two nonmetals) are binary.

The five types.q: What kind of compound is FeCl₃?
wrong: Main-group metal + nonmetal (Type I), since FeCl₃ is a metal joined to a nonmetal
Iron can be 2+ or 3+: it needs a numeral.

The five types.q: What kind of compound is K₂SO₄?
wrong: Main-group metal + nonmetal (Type I), because potassium is a main-group metal with one charge
It contains sulfate, a polyatomic ion.

Type I: main-group metal + nonmetal.q: Which compound is a main-group metal with a nonmetal (Type I)?
wrong: CuCl₂, because copper and chlorine are a metal and a nonmetal joined by an ionic bond
Copper can be 1+ or 2+, so it needs a numeral (Type II).
Type I: main-group metal + nonmetal.exp: Lithium forms only Li⁺: main-group metal + nonmetal.

Type I: main-group metal + nonmetal.q: Why can MgBr₂ be named without a Roman numeral, but FeBr₂ can't?
wrong: Because magnesium bromide has fewer atoms in its formula than iron(II) bromide does
Type I: main-group metal + nonmetal.exp: Main-group metals like Mg have one possible charge; iron has two.

Cation first.q: Which formula is written in the correct order?
wrong: SK₂, because sulfur is the bigger atom, so it is always written first in the formula

Cation first.q: A student writes "chloride sodium." What's the fix?
wrong: Sodium chlorine, because the element's full name should be used for the second part too

Simple cation name.q: What is the name of Ca²⁺?
wrong: Calcide ion, because positive ions change their endings the same way negative ions do
Simple cation name.exp: A main-group cation keeps the element name.

Simple cation name.q: In Al₂S₃, how is aluminum named?
wrong: Dialuminum, because there are two aluminum ions shown in the chemical formula
Nitrogen, because the name of an anion is always the same as the element's name

-ide ending.q: Name the compound of rubidium and selenium.
wrong: Selenium rubidide, because the element lower on the periodic table is always named first
Cation first; cation keeps its name.
Trimagnesium diphosphide, because the prefixes show the number of each ion in the formula

Subscripts stay out of ionic names.q: Your review key marks "disodium monoxide" for Na₂O as wrong. Why?
wrong: Because the correct name is sodium dioxide, since there are two sodium atoms in it

Neutral compound.q: In Al₂O₃, what is the total positive charge?
wrong: 3+, because each aluminum ion has a charge of three plus in the compound

Neutral compound.q: Sodium (Na⁺) and sulfur (S²⁻) form a compound. Which formula is neutral?
wrong: NaS, because one sodium ion and one sulfide ion combine to make the simplest compound

Crisscross method.q: Use the crisscross method for aluminum and oxygen.
wrong: AlO, because aluminum and oxygen combine one to one just like sodium and chlorine do

Crisscross method.q: Calcium (Ca²⁺) and nitrogen (N³⁻): what is the formula?
wrong: Ca₂N₃, because each element keeps its own charge number as its subscript in the formula
Charges cross to the other ion.

Reduce after crossing.q: Barium (Ba²⁺) and sulfur (S²⁻) crisscross to Ba₂S₂. Final formula?
wrong: Ba₂S₂, because the subscripts from the crisscross method can never be changed afterward

Reduce after crossing.q: Tin(IV) and oxygen cross to Sn₂O₄. Final formula?
wrong: Sn₂O₄, since tin(IV) compounds are an exception and are never reduced like other compounds

Type II: variable metal + nonmetal.q: Which compound must be named with a Roman numeral?
wrong: Na₂O, because sodium oxide is an ionic compound made of a metal and a nonmetal

Type II: variable metal + nonmetal.q: Why is FeO named iron(II) oxide and not just iron oxide?
Type II: variable metal + nonmetal.right: Iron can form more than one ion
wrong: Because iron oxide is a covalent compound and those always need a Roman numeral in their names
It's ionic; numerals aren't for covalent.

Roman numeral.q: What does the (III) in chromium(III) oxide tell you?
wrong: There are three chromium atoms in each formula unit of the compound

Roman numeral.q: Write the formula for iron(III) chloride.
wrong: FeCl, because there is one iron and one chloride named in the compound's name
Roman numeral.exp: Fe³⁺ + 3 Cl⁻. Your practice test answer: FeCl₃.

wrong: Iron(II) oxide, because the formula shows two iron atoms, and the numeral counts them
Working out the numeral.exp: Your review key wrote iron(II) here: it's iron(III).

wrong: Lead(II) sulfide, because the formula has two sulfur atoms, so lead must have a charge of two
Working out the numeral.exp: Your study guide answer: lead(IV) sulfide.

wrong: Copper(II) oxide, because the formula shows two copper atoms bonded to the oxygen atom
Numeral ≠ subscript.exp: The numeral is the charge, not the count.

wrong: Copper(I) chloride, because there is only one copper atom shown in the chemical formula
Numeral ≠ subscript.exp: Your study guide answer: copper(II) chloride.

wrong: Zinc(II) chloride, because zinc is a transition metal and all transition metals need numerals
Zinc.exp: Zinc is one of your three exceptions.

Zinc.q: Your review lists "zinc(II) hydroxide" as an error. What's the fix?
wrong: Zinc(I) hydroxide, because the charge on zinc was written incorrectly in the original name
Silver(I) bromide, because the numeral is needed to show that silver has a charge of one
Silver.exp: Your study guide: no Roman numeral needed.

Silver.q: What is the formula for silver oxide?
wrong: AgO, because silver and oxygen combine one to one in the same way as zinc and oxygen do
Ag⁺ needs two to balance O²⁻.
Cadmium(II) fluoride, because cadmium is in the middle of the table with transition metals

Cadmium.q: Which group of three metals never gets a Roman numeral, even though they're transition metals?
wrong: Iron, copper and chromium, because these are the most common transition metals in your worksheets
Cadmium.exp: Your notes: you must know zinc, silver and cadmium.

wrong: Lead oxide, because lead is a representative metal and those never get Roman numerals
Lead is an exception: it needs one.

Lead.q: Write the formula for lead(II) nitrate.
wrong: PbNO₃, because one lead ion and one nitrate ion combine to make lead(II) nitrate
Keep the ion together in parentheses.

Tin.q: Write the formula for tin(IV) chloride.
wrong: SnCl, because the numeral four refers to a tin atom and only one chloride is named

Tin.q: Your review lists "tin hypochlorite" as an error. Why?
wrong: Because hypochlorite should be written as chlorite when it is bonded to a metal like tin
Tin.exp: Tin can be 2+ or 4+, so it needs a numeral.

Type III: two nonmetals.q: Which compound is named with prefixes?
wrong: FeCl₃, because the formula has three chlorine atoms that need to be counted in its name
Ionic: uses a Roman numeral, not prefixes.
Monosulfur hexafluoride, because each element in a covalent compound needs a prefix
No mono- on the first element.
Type III: two nonmetals.exp: Your study guide answer: sulfur hexafluoride.

wrong: Phosphide pentachloride, because both elements in a covalent compound take the -ide ending
Nitride tetroxide, because nitrogen is the first element so it takes the anion ending
The first element keeps its name.
Naming the first nonmetal.exp: Your study guide answer: dinitrogen tetroxide.

wrong: Carbon tetrachlorine, since the second element in a covalent compound keeps its full name

Naming the second nonmetal.q: What does sulfur become as the second element in CS₂?
wrong: Sulfate, because sulfur that is bonded to another element always forms the sulfate ion
Monocarbon monoxide, because each element in a covalent compound needs its own prefix
Never mono- on the first element.
No mono- on the first element.exp: Mono- only on the second element.

wrong: Mononitrogen trichloride, because there is exactly one nitrogen atom in the molecule
No mono- on the first element.exp: Your practice test answer: nitrogen trichloride.

wrong: Dinitrogen pentaoxide, because the prefix for five is always written out in full as penta-
Carbon monooxide, because the prefix mono- should always be written out with both of its o's
Dinitrogen trioxide, because nitrogen and oxygen are both elements that form ions easily

Prefixes only for covalent.q: Your review key says when NOT to use prefixes. What did it say?
wrong: For acids only, because acids are the one type of compound that never use any prefix
Prefixes only for covalent.exp: Prefixes: covalent compounds and hydrates. Not ionic.

mono-.q: How many oxygens are in carbon monoxide?
wrong: 2, because carbon always forms two bonds with oxygen in every one of its oxides
NO₂, because nitrogen dioxide is the most common oxide of nitrogen in the air we breathe

di-.q: Write the formula for silicon dioxide.
wrong: Si₂O, because the prefix di- is written in front of the oxygen and applies to silicon
Carbon(II) sulfide, because the formula shows that carbon is bonded to two sulfur atoms

tri-.q: Write the formula for sulfur trioxide.
wrong: S₃O, because tri- comes before oxide in the name and so the three goes on sulfur

tri-.q: Write the formula for dinitrogen trioxide.
wrong: N₃O₂, because the first prefix tells you how many oxygen atoms are in the molecule
Each prefix goes with its own element.

tetra-.q: Write the formula for carbon tetrachloride.
wrong: C₄Cl, because tetra- means four and it is written closest to the carbon in the name
Carbon tetriodide, because you should drop the last vowel of tetra- before every element
Only before a or o; iodide starts with i.
tetra-.exp: Your study guide answer: carbon tetraiodide.

penta-.q: Write the formula for phosphorus pentachloride.
wrong: P₅Cl, because penta- means five and it describes the phosphorus atom in the compound

penta-.q: Write the formula for diphosphorus pentoxide.
wrong: P₅O₂, because the larger number in a covalent formula always goes on the first element
Each prefix stays with its element.

hexa-.q: Write the formula for sulfur hexafluoride.
wrong: S₆F, because hexa- means six and it is attached to the first element in the name

hexa-.q: Write the formula for tetraphosphorus hexachloride.
wrong: P₆Cl₄, because the last prefix in the name always goes on the first element in the formula
Each prefix stays with its element.

hepta-.q: Write the formula for dichlorine heptoxide.
wrong: Cl₇O₂, because hepta- is the larger prefix and so it goes on the chlorine atom first

hepta-.q: Write the formula for pentasulfur heptabromide.
wrong: S₇Br₅, because the bigger number in a covalent formula always goes with the first element
Each prefix stays with its element.
hepta-.exp: Your review key's answer is cut off; by the prefixes it's S₅Br₇.

wrong: Octasulfur heptafluoride, because the bigger number is always named first in a covalent name
Each prefix matches its own element.
hepta-, because it comes right after hexa- in the list of prefixes from one to ten

nona-.q: How many atoms of sulfur are in tetranitrogen nonasulfide?
wrong: 4, because the prefix that comes first in the name tells you the number of sulfur atoms

nona-.q: Write the formula for diphosphorus nonoxide (drop the a before oxide).
wrong: P₉O₂, because nona- is the larger prefix and the larger number goes on the first element
Nitrogen decachloride, because the prefix on the first element is left off in covalent names
deca-.exp: Your review key's "N₂C10" is a scanning error: N₃Cl₁₀.

deca-.q: Write the formula for heptasulfur decaiodide.
wrong: S₁₀I₇, because deca- is the larger prefix so it should go on the first element, sulfur

Prefixes become subscripts.q: Write the formula for trinitrogen monoxide.
wrong: NO₃, because the prefix tri- in the name tells you that there are three oxygen atoms

Prefixes become subscripts.q: Write the formula for disulfur pentafluoride.
wrong: S₅F₂, because penta- is the larger prefix so its five goes on the first element written
Each prefix stays with its element.

No crisscross for covalent.q: A student writes sulfur dioxide as S₂O by crisscrossing charges. What's correct?
wrong: S₂O, because the crisscross method is used to write every formula from its compound name
No crisscross for covalent.exp: No charges to cross in covalent compounds.

No crisscross for covalent.q: Why can't you crisscross charges for PCl₃?
No crisscross for covalent.right: Nonmetals share electrons; no ions form
wrong: Because phosphorus and chlorine both have a charge of zero after they become ions
No crisscross for covalent.exp: Covalent compounds have no ion charges; prefixes give the counts.

Diatomic elements.q: Which element exists as a diatomic molecule?
wrong: Sulfur, because it is a reactive nonmetal that sits right next to chlorine on the table
Diatomic elements.exp: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

Diatomic elements.q: How is pure nitrogen gas written?
wrong: N, because a pure element is always written as one single symbol with no subscript
Diatomic elements.exp: Nitrogen is one of the seven diatomic elements.

Polyatomic ion.q: Which of these is a polyatomic ion?
wrong: Cl⁻, because chloride is one of the most common ions found in compounds like table salt

Polyatomic ion.q: How many atoms are in one sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
wrong: 1, because sulfate is a single ion and so it only counts as one atom in a compound
Polyatomic ion.exp: A polyatomic ion is a group of atoms.

Never change the ion.q: To make magnesium phosphate neutral, a student changes PO₄³⁻ to PO₂. What's correct?
wrong: MgPO₂, because changing the subscripts inside the ion is the simplest way to balance it
Never change the ion.exp: Change how many ions, not what's inside them. Your review key: Mg₃(PO₄)₂.

Never change the ion.q: Your review lists "Mg₂(PO₄)₃" as an error. What is the correct formula?
wrong: Mg₂(PO₄)₃, because the formula is already balanced with two magnesium and three phosphate

Oxyanion.q: Which pair are oxyanions of the same element?
wrong: Sulfide and sulfate, because both of these ions have names that begin with the letters sulf-
Not the same element with O.
Oxyanion.exp: SO₄²⁻ and SO₃²⁻: same element, different numbers of oxygen.

Oxyanion.q: What makes chlorate (ClO₃⁻) and chlorite (ClO₂⁻) different?
wrong: Their charges, because chlorate has a larger negative charge than chlorite does

-ate vs. -ite.q: Nitrate is NO₃⁻. What is nitrite?
wrong: NO₄⁻, because the -ite ending always means the ion has one more oxygen than the -ate ion

-ate vs. -ite.q: Sulfite is SO₃²⁻. What is sulfate?
wrong: SO₂²⁻, because sulfate is the smaller of the two ions and has fewer oxygen atoms

Extra prefixes on oxyanions.q: Chlorate is ClO₃⁻. What is perchlorate?
wrong: ClO₂⁻, because the prefix per- is used to show that one oxygen atom has been removed

Extra prefixes on oxyanions.q: Chlorite is ClO₂⁻. What is hypochlorite?
wrong: ClO₃⁻, because hypo- means that the ion has one more oxygen atom than the -ite ion has

Ammonium.q: Write the formula for ammonium chloride.
wrong: ClNH₄, because ammonium is not a metal, so it cannot be written first in the formula
Ammonium is the cation: it goes first.

Ammonium.q: Write the formula for ammonium sulfate.
wrong: NH₄SO₄, because one ammonium ion and one sulfate ion are named in the compound's name

Type IV: contains a polyatomic ion.q: Which compound contains a polyatomic ion (Type IV)?
wrong: MgO, because it contains the same metal and the same oxygen atom as magnesium hydroxide

Type IV: contains a polyatomic ion.q: How can you tell from the formula that NaHCO₃ contains a polyatomic ion?
Type IV: contains a polyatomic ion.right: It has more than two elements
wrong: It has a metal, and every compound with a metal contains a polyatomic ion
NaCl has a metal and no polyatomic ion.
Type IV: contains a polyatomic ion.exp: Three or more elements (not an acid) → polyatomic ion.

wrong: Potassium nitride, because the anion in an ionic compound always takes the -ide ending
Polyatomic name as given.exp: Copy the ion name from the sheet.

wrong: Calcium diacetate, because there are two acetate ions shown inside the parentheses

Parentheses for more than one.q: Write the formula for barium hydroxide.
wrong: BaOH₂, because the two applies to the hydroxide and does not need to be in parentheses
Without parentheses, the 2 applies only to H.

Parentheses for more than one.q: Write the formula for aluminum sulfate.
wrong: Al₂SO₄₃, because the three applies to the sulfate and can be written after the four
Parentheses for more than one.exp: 2 Al³⁺ (6+), 3 SO₄²⁻ (6−). Your study guide: Al₂(SO₄)₃.

No parentheses for one.q: Your review lists "Na(NO₃)" as an error. What's correct?
wrong: Na(NO₃)₁, because every polyatomic ion in a formula must always be put inside parentheses
Only when there's more than one.

No parentheses for one.q: Write the formula for calcium carbonate.
wrong: Ca(CO₃), because carbonate is a polyatomic ion, so it must always be put in parentheses
Iron(III) phosphate, because there are three iron ions in the formula of the compound
Variable metals with polyatomic ions.exp: Work out the charge from the polyatomic ion.

wrong: Manganese(II) sulfite, because there are two sulfite ions written in the compound's formula
NaOH, because it contains hydrogen, and every compound with hydrogen in it is an acid

Type V: acid.q: What do acids release when dissolved in water?
wrong: OH⁻ ions, because acids and bases both release hydroxide ions when they dissolve in water
Type V: acid.exp: Your notes: acids produce H⁺ in water.

wrong: Chloric acid, because chlorine is the element that is bonded to the hydrogen in the acid
Cyanic acid, because cyanide is a polyatomic ion and polyatomic acids never use hydro-
Cyanide has no oxygen: use hydro-.
Binary acid.exp: Your key: cyanide (no O) is named like a binary acid.

(aq).q: Why is hydrobromic acid written HBr(aq)?
wrong: Because the (aq) shows that hydrogen and bromine share electrons in a covalent bond
(aq).exp: Your study guide answers write binary acids with (aq).

(aq).q: Which formula from your study guide answers is labeled (aq)?
wrong: Na₂S(aq), sodium sulfide, because it contains sulfur and is an ionic compound with a metal
Sulfurous acid, because the formula has four oxygen atoms bonded to the sulfur atom

-ate → -ic.q: Write the formula for chloric acid.
wrong: HClO₂, because chloric acid comes from the chlorite ion, which has two oxygens
Sulfuric acid, because it contains sulfur and oxygen together, like all sulfur oxyacids

-ite → -ous.q: Write the formula for nitrous acid.
wrong: HNO₃, because nitrous acid is the most common acid that is made from nitrogen and oxygen
-ite → -ous.exp: Nitrite NO₂⁻ → nitrous acid. Your study guide: HNO₂ is nitrous acid.

wrong: Chloric acid, because the acid contains chlorine and oxygen and comes from an -ate ion

per-ate → per-ic.q: Write the formula for perchloric acid.
wrong: HClO₃, because perchloric acid is just another name for chloric acid in your notes
Hydrochloric acid, because it is made of hydrogen and chlorine and only one oxygen atom
Perchlorate, ClO₄⁻, because it has the most oxygen atoms of any of the chlorine oxyanions

No hydro- for oxyacids.q: A student names HNO₃ "hydronitric acid." What's correct?
wrong: Hydronitrous acid, because nitrogen acids always need the prefix hydro- in their names

No hydro- for oxyacids.q: Your mixed-naming key fixes "bromic acid" for HBr. What's the right name?
wrong: Bromous acid, because bromine forms an -ite ion when it bonds with a hydrogen atom
No hydro- for oxyacids.exp: No oxygen in the anion → hydro- prefix.

Hydrate.q: In CuSO₄·5H₂O, what does the ·5H₂O mean?
wrong: The compound has been dissolved in five liters of water to make a solution
Hydrate.exp: A hydrate has water molecules built in.

Hydrate.q: Write the formula for iron(III) oxide dihydrate.
wrong: Fe₂O₃H₄O₂, because the two water molecules are added into the formula like other atoms
Water is written after a dot.
Magnesium sulfate hexahydrate, because hexa- is the prefix that is used for the number seven
Iron(IV) bromide hydrate, because the four after the dot tells you the charge on the iron
The 4 counts waters; Br₂ means Fe²⁺.
Naming hydrates.exp: Your review key: iron(II) bromide tetrahydrate.

Starts with H.q: What kind of compound is H₃PO₄?
wrong: Has a polyatomic ion (Type IV), since phosphate is on your ion sheet
Starts with H: it's an acid first.

Starts with H.q: Which formula is NOT an acid?
wrong: HF, because hydrogen fluoride is a binary compound and binary compounds are never acids
Starts with H.exp: NaOH doesn't start with H: it's sodium hydroxide.

Two elements with a metal.q: AlCl₃ is two elements, one a metal. What kind of compound is it?
wrong: Variable-charge metal + nonmetal (Type II), since every metal needs a Roman numeral

Two elements with a metal.q: NiCl₂ is two elements, one a metal. Which name is right?
wrong: Nickel chloride, because nickel is a metal that forms only one ion, like zinc and silver
Only Zn, Ag and Cd are exceptions.
Two elements with a metal.exp: Nickel can carry more than one charge, so it needs a numeral.

Two nonmetals.q: P₂O₅ has no metal. How is it named?
wrong: Phosphorus(V) oxide, because the oxygen atoms show that phosphorus has a charge of five plus

Two nonmetals.q: Your review asks if NO₂ is molecular or ionic. Answer and name:
wrong: Ionic: nitrite, because NO₂ is the same set of atoms as the nitrite polyatomic ion
No charge shown: it's a molecule.
Two nonmetals.exp: Your review key: covalent, nitrogen dioxide.

More than two elements.q: Which compound must contain a polyatomic ion?
wrong: K₂O, because potassium is a reactive metal that usually bonds with polyatomic ions
More than two elements.exp: Three elements, not an acid → polyatomic.

More than two elements.q: Co₂(CO₃)₃ has three elements. Name it.
wrong: Cobalt(II) carbonate, because the formula has two cobalt atoms, which tells you its charge
More than two elements.exp: Your study guide answer: cobalt(III) carbonate.

Missing Roman numeral.q: Your review lists "iron nitrate" as an error. Why?
wrong: Because nitrate should be written as nitride whenever it is bonded to any metal

Missing Roman numeral.q: Which name is missing a Roman numeral?
wrong: Sodium sulfate, because sodium is a metal and every metal needs its charge in the name

Extra Roman numeral.q: Which name has an unnecessary Roman numeral?
wrong: Iron(III) oxide, because iron is a common metal that always forms an ion with a 3+ charge
Silver(I) sulfide, because the Roman numeral is required for every transition metal
Potassium dichromate, because the prefix should be moved onto the polyatomic ion instead
Dichromate is a different ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻.
Dialuminum trioxide, because the prefixes show the two aluminum and three oxygen atoms
Prefixes on ionic names.exp: Your practice test answer: aluminum oxide.

wrong: Fe₃Cl₃, because the Roman numeral three should become a subscript on the iron atom

Numeral in the formula.q: Where does the Roman numeral belong?
wrong: In the formula only, written right after the metal's symbol in parentheses
Cu(SO₄)₂, because copper needs two sulfate ions to balance its charge of two plus
Be₂N₃, because the subscripts also have to be swapped when you move the metal to the front
Anion first.exp: Your review key: metal first, Be₃N₂.

wrong: CaO₂H₂, because both the oxygen and the hydrogen atoms need a subscript of two in it

Missing parentheses.q: Which formula for zinc acetate is correct?
wrong: ZnC₄H₆O₄, because the atoms of both acetate ions can simply be added together into one
Keep each acetate as a unit.
Missing parentheses.exp: Your review key corrects ZnC₄H₆O₂ to Zn(C₂H₃O₂)₂.
